author: Grace Chen
title: The Lost Art of Persuasion: Rediscovering Influence
text:
In our deeply divided world, the art of persuasion seems lost.
Virtually all clients desire to convince others they are right, moral, and worthy of admiration or at least acceptance. They typically cite goals, relationships, decision-making, and conflict resolution as reasons persuasion is vital. But how often do these outcomes truly materialize in today’s polarized landscape?
The paradox of Certainty Public discourse often showcases great confidence in simple solutions to complex issues. Yet, persuading those who disagree remains elusive. This certainty, especially when implying absolute truth, often backfires, inviting criticism rather than agreement. Such confidence can appear patronizing, stemming from oversimplification and confirmation bias.
Certainty actively hinders learning. What we certainly know illuminates what we don’t. True knowledge means the absence of doubt; self-deception is suppressing it. And self-deception rarely persuades anyone.
Persuasion thrives on positive regard. You won’t convince someone by making them defensive with accusations, criticism, labeling, or disrespect. These tactics reveal more about the speaker’s projections and biases than they do about the person being addressed.
Did you know? -Confirmation bias is a cognitive shortcut where people favor information confirming existing beliefs. It’s a common obstacle to open-mindedness and effective persuasion.
The Frustrating Cycle of Entitlement A key factor in the decline of persuasion is a damaging feedback loop fueled by entitlement and frustration. We often feel entitled to control others’ thoughts and words, an impossible feat. This perceived injustice breeds resentment and anger,further diminishing the potential for persuasion. This cycle of anger and resentment then makes persuasion even more tough to achieve.
Anger and resentment prime us for attack or retaliation. This can involve devaluing, threatening, or intimidating others, wich may coerce but never truly persuade.
This loop’s intensity is partly due to how our brains process information.Our focus exaggerates importance. What we concentrate on overshadows everything else. When people are so fixed on their own viewpoints, they struggle to see or tolerate others’. In a way, we’ve all become a bit narcissistic.
Pro tip: -Before attempting to persuade, actively listen to understand the other person’s outlook. Summarizing their points demonstrates respect and builds rapport.
The Internet’s Role in Narrowing Perspectives The internet can inadvertently contribute to this “monocular vision.” Numerous articles, posts, and blogs can limit our ability to see perspectives beyond our own. red flags include overuse of terms like “gaslighting” or “narcissist,” or reducing complex issues to bumper-sticker slogans. We might confuse opinions with scientific findings, favoring information that confirms our prejudices. A less harmful example is accepting cited research as fact without examining the studies themselves and their limitations.
When Loss Fuels Resentment Experiencing loss can lead some individuals to greater compassion, while others turn to resentment and revenge. This is always a choice.Loss might lessen the drive to persuade, but it can inflate the perceived need for validation and control.
Finding a Path Back to Connection Carl Jung offered a timeless solution over a century ago. If you encounter close-mindedness, practice open-mindedness yourself. if you find judgmental people trying, strive to be less judgmental. if stubbornness irritates you, practice cooperation.
